source.title: Understanding the Money Laundering Risks in the Capital Markets - Thematic Review TR19/4

summary: FCA thematic review of money-laundering risk across UK secondary (and, to a lesser extent, primary) capital markets, based on visits to 19 participants. It finds CDD, transaction-chain visibility and SAR reporting weaknesses, and sets out a non-exhaustive Annex of seven illustrative, fictionalised typologies - free-of-payment securities movement, mirror trading, MTN debt issuance, discounted equity placement to a connected investor, omnibus/reliance intermediation, FX option premium layering, and account over-collateralisation/dormant cash withdrawal - plus a list of trade-level red flags for transaction monitoring and training.

citations.quote: Some market -abuse practices (eg wash trading) may also be indicative of money laundering.
The result is that both customers are flat in the security, ie neither had net bought or sold. However, money has moved from the customer in Country A to the customer in Country B.
The FCA’s Final Notice to Deutsche Bank in January 2017 is another example of mirror trading off-market.

typologies.label: Free of Payment Securities Transfer Laundering

citations.quote: Company A then requests that the government bonds are transferred into the newly formed account at Broker 2. Broker 2 accepts the government bonds into the customer’s portfolio, without speaking to Broker 1 about their origin or ownership.
Company A has realised clean cash in Country 2.
IB1 does not have sight of, or conduct due diligence on, the end investor but receives assurances from Company A that due diligence has been done.
The arrangement suggests a strong link between the borrower and underlying “lender” which could indicate potential embezzlement, money laundering or both.
This individual has connections with a senior director of the company, though this was not disclosed publicly.

It appears the activity was undertaken to wash illicit funds through the markets (and cross-jurisdiction) by lending money to the company, which was exchanged for shares that can be sold for more than the value of the loan.

The UK-based bank does not treat the offshore broker as high-risk and therefore does not conduct EDD. The UK-based bank also relies on the offshore broker, as a regulated firm, to do CDD on its customers.

As such, the bank has potentially been facilitating the transfer of economic value from one account to another, cross-jurisdiction, without realising that this might have been linked to financial crime.

The effect of the activity is that the customer receives an initial premium payment into their prime brokerage account at a separate bank, only for this to be paid back upon the almost immediate expiry of the FX options.
The neutralising effect of the trading raises concerns that the intended purpose is to facilitate the layering stage of a money-laundering scheme.
The excess collateral is returned to the customer, but no questions are asked.
it seems plausible that the cash was simply entered and withdrawn to make it appear cleaner.

indicators.description: 'Free of payment' asset transfers between accounts/brokers, particularly before onward sale of the asset.

citations.quote: ‘free of payment’ asset transfers

indicators.description: Remote booking of trades between group entities, executed in one jurisdiction and booked via an overseas branch into another.

citations.quote: remote booking of trades between group entities

indicators.description: Pre-arranged trading where buy and sell counterparties are specified and already agreed before execution.

citations.quote: pre-arranged trading

indicators.description: Instructions to trade coming from, or involvement of, unconnected third parties rather than the account holder.

citations.quote: instructions or involvement from third parties

indicators.description: Non-standard settlement arrangements that deviate from a customer's usual instructions, e.g. delivery into a third-party broker account.

citations.quote: We refer to settlement arrangements as being ‘non-standard’ in the context of a particular customer’s usual trading and settlement.

indicators.description: Uneconomic or irrational trading strategies with no apparent business or economic rationale.

citations.quote: uneconomic or irrational trading strategies of a customer

indicators.description: Counterparty concentration, where a customer trades repeatedly and almost exclusively against the same counterparty.

citations.quote: counterparty concentration

indicators.description: Unusually high or consistent win/loss rates, or flat/neutralising trading activity that ends a position at no net gain or loss.

citations.quote: unusual win/loss rates or flat/neutralising activity

indicators.description: Dormant accounts with no trading activity, sometimes followed by a significant cash withdrawal to a third party.

citations.quote: no trading on an account
The customer does not then trade on the account. Instead, two months later, it withdraws the cash to a third-party account.

indicators.description: Settlement instructions or involvement of accounts located in jurisdictions classified as posing high money-laundering risk.

citations.quote: Settlement into high-risk jurisdictions is a risk factor that we observed some participants starting to include within their automated monitoring processes.

indicators.description: Ultimate beneficial ownership of a deposited or transferred financial instrument is not verified before it is accepted into a customer's account.

citations.quote: no checks take place to determine the ultimate beneficial owner of the bonds

indicators.description: Firm has no visibility of its customer's own underlying customers or the ultimate beneficial owner of assets traded, common in chains involving omnibus accounts or reliance.

citations.quote: We found that most participants had no visibility of their customer’s customer or, for example, the ultimate beneficial owner of the asset being traded.

extraction_notes: Document is a broad FCA thematic review rather than a single-scheme alert; its Annex (pp.19-29) explicitly states the seven worked typology examples are illustrative composites 'modified and developed with fictitious information' from a variety of intelligence sources (page 19, para 2), not confirmed live cases (except the Deutsche Bank mirror-trading references, which are real). Four of the seven typologies (Free of Payment Securities Transfer, MTN/Debt Issuance Layering, Omnibus/Reliance Intermediation, Account Funding Layering) had no above-floor Knowledge Centre match and are proposed as emergent; reviewers should sanity-check these against any newer capital-markets doctrine. CM005 (Wash Trading) and BA008 (Layering) are cross-purpose links (market-abuse and correspondent-banking doctrine respectively) selected as the closest functional fit for the mirror-trading and option-premium examples - the document itself draws the wash-trading/ML parallel at para 2.24. PAT009 sits in the network family; confirm desk routing accordingly. Only one real (named) actor - Deutsche Bank - appears; all other entities in the Annex (Company A, Broker 1/2/3 etc.) are explicitly fictitious illustrations and were not extracted as actors.
